introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c)**

(a) (i) Define work function. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine Planck's constant. Your description should include a diagram, procedure, precaution, observation and a conclusion. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Work function.** The work function $\phi$ of a metal is the **minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the metal** (to take it from inside the metal to just outside, with zero kinetic energy). It is equal to $hf_0$, where $f_0$ is the threshold frequency.

**(ii) Experiment: stopping potential of a photocell.**

**Apparatus and diagram (described).** A **vacuum photocell** (photoemissive cathode and collecting anode in an evacuated tube with a quartz or glass window) is illuminated by a lamp through a set of **narrow-band (interference) filters** or by monochromatic light from a monochromator, of known frequencies $f$. The anode is connected through a **potential divider** (rheostat across a battery, with a reversing switch) so that the anode can be made **negative** with respect to the cathode (a retarding p.d.). A **voltmeter** reads the p.d. $V$ between the electrodes and a sensitive **micro-ammeter (or electrometer)** in the cell circuit detects the photocurrent.

**Procedure.**

1. Shine light of the first (known) frequency $f$ on the cathode and read the photocurrent with zero p.d.
2. Increase the retarding p.d. gradually until the micro-ammeter reading **just falls to zero**. Record this **stopping potential** $V_s$.
3. Repeat with filters of other frequencies (at least six), recording $f$ and $V_s$ each time.
4. Plot a graph of $V_s$ (vertical axis) against $f$ (horizontal axis).

**Observation.** For each frequency above a certain minimum value, a stopping p.d. exists; $V_s$ **increases linearly** with the frequency of the light. The graph is a straight line which cuts the frequency axis at the **threshold frequency** $f_0$ (below $f_0$ there is no photocurrent, however bright the light). Changing the intensity of the light changes the size of the photocurrent but **not** $V_s$.

**Conclusion.** The most energetic emitted electrons have kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv_{\max}^2 = eV_s$. Einstein's photoelectric equation $hf = \phi + eV_s$ gives
$$V_s = \frac{h}{e}\,f - \frac{\phi}{e}.$$
So the **gradient** of the graph of $V_s$ against $f$ equals $h/e$, and
$$h = e\times\text{gradient}.$$
The value obtained is close to $6.6\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$. The intercept on the vertical axis gives $-\phi/e$ and the intercept on the frequency axis gives $f_0 = \phi/h$.

**Precautions.**

- Carry out the experiment in a **darkened room** and shield the cell from stray light, so that only the filtered light reaches the cathode.
- Keep the **lamp-cell distance and the lamp supply constant** so that the photocurrent is steady; wait for steady readings.
- Use a **sensitive** current detector and approach the zero-current point slowly, reading $V_s$ carefully at the point where the current just disappears.
- Use a voltmeter of **very high resistance** so that it does not draw current from the divider.
- Keep the cell **clean and free from contamination** (surface oxide changes the work function).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) State the laws of electromagnetic induction. *[4 marks]*

(ii) A coil of area $0.25\ \mathrm{m^2}$ with $100$ turns is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of $3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T}$. Calculate the magnetic flux linkage in the coil. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Laws of electromagnetic induction.**

- **Faraday's law:** the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is **directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage** (the rate at which magnetic flux is cut by the conductor): $\mathcal{E} = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(N\Phi)}{\mathrm{d}t}$.
- **Lenz's law:** the direction of the induced e.m.f. (and of the induced current) is such that it **opposes the change** that produces it (this expresses conservation of energy, and is the meaning of the minus sign).

**(ii) Flux linkage.** The coil is at right angles to the field: its plane is perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, so the field is along the normal to the coil and the flux through each turn is $\Phi = BA$.
$$N\Phi = NBA = 100\times3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T}\times0.25\ \mathrm{m^2} = 7.5\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}.$$

**The magnetic flux linkage is $7.5\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$ (weber-turns)**; the flux through one turn is $7.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Calculate the period of rotation of the moon round the earth if the mean radius of the moon's orbit is $3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State one difference between the magnetic force and the gravitational force. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Period of the moon.** Constants (not printed in the paper): $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}$ and mass of the earth $M = 5.98\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

The gravitational attraction of the earth supplies the centripetal force for the moon of mass $m$:
$$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = m\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 r \;\Rightarrow\; T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GM}.$$
$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(3.0\times10^{8})^3}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times5.98\times10^{24}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2.7\times10^{25}}{3.99\times10^{14}}}$$
$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{6.77\times10^{10}} = 2\pi\times2.60\times10^{5} = 1.63\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s}\quad(\approx 18.9\ \text{days}).$$

**$T \approx 1.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s}$** for the radius printed in the question. (The real mean radius, $3.84\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$, would give about $27.4$ days.)

**(ii) One difference.** The **gravitational force is always attractive**, whereas the **magnetic force can be attractive or repulsive** (depending on the poles or on the directions of the currents). (Other acceptable differences: gravity acts on every mass, but the magnetic force acts only on moving charges, currents or magnetic materials; the magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR 6 (d), (e) and (f)**

(d) (i) Define specific latent heat of vaporisation. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. Your description should include a diagram, procedure, precaution, observation and a conclusion. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Specific latent heat of vaporisation.** It is the **quantity of heat energy required to change unit mass ($1\ \mathrm{kg}$) of a substance from the liquid to the vapour state at constant temperature** (its boiling point). Unit: $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

**(ii) Experiment: continuous-flow electrical method with a condenser.**

**Apparatus and diagram (described).** A well **lagged** vessel (a vacuum flask or a lagged calorimeter) holds water and an **electric immersion heater** connected to a supply through an ammeter and a voltmeter (or a joulemeter) and a rheostat, so that the power $P = VI$ is known. The vessel is closed by a lid carrying a thermometer and a **delivery tube** leading the steam into a **condenser** (a Liebig condenser or a cold tube); a **beaker on a balance** collects the condensed water.

**Procedure.**

1. Switch on the heater and bring the water to the boil; wait until it boils **steadily** and condensed water drips into the beaker at a constant rate, so that the apparatus has reached a steady state.
2. Place a dry beaker of known mass under the condenser, start a stopwatch, and read $V$ and $I$.
3. After a measured time $t$ (for example $10\ \text{min}$), remove the beaker and find the mass $m_1$ of water collected; note the power $P_1 = V_1I_1$.
4. Repeat with the **same time** $t$ but a different heater power $P_2 = V_2I_2$ (adjust the rheostat), collecting a mass $m_2$.

**Observation.** The mass of water collected in the same time is larger for the larger heating power.

**Conclusion.** The energy supplied by the heater in time $t$ is used partly to vaporise the water and partly lost to the surroundings (the heat-loss rate $H$ is the same in both runs, since the water boils at the same temperature):
$$P_1t = m_1L + Ht,\qquad P_2t = m_2L + Ht.$$
Subtracting eliminates the unknown loss $Ht$:
$$L = \frac{(P_1 - P_2)\,t}{m_1 - m_2}.$$
The result is close to $2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. (Without the second run, and with good lagging, $L \approx Pt/m$.)

**Precautions.**

- **Lag** the vessel and the delivery tube to reduce heat losses (and keep losses the same in both runs).
- Wait for **steady boiling** before collecting, so that the water collected corresponds to steam produced during the measurement.
- Keep the heater **fully immersed** and ensure that no water spray or boiling droplets are carried over into the condenser.
- Start and stop the collection and the stopwatch at the same instant; use the **same time** in both runs.
- Keep the voltage and current **constant** during each run and read them regularly.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) State Kirchhoff's laws for electric circuits. *[4 marks]*

(ii) Consider the circuit diagram in figure 2.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

Determine the reading of the ammeter when light of constant intensity falls on the light dependent resistor (LDR) and the voltmeter reads $4\ \mathrm{V}$. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Kirchhoff's laws.**

- **First law (junction rule):** the **sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it** (the algebraic sum of the currents at a junction is zero). It expresses the **conservation of electric charge**.
- **Second law (loop rule):** around any **closed loop** of a circuit, the **algebraic sum of the e.m.f.s equals the algebraic sum of the products $IR$** (the potential drops) in that loop. It expresses the **conservation of energy**.

**(ii) Ammeter reading.** The LDR and the $50\ \Omega$ resistor are in series with the $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery and the ammeter; the voltmeter is connected across the LDR. We take the battery to have negligible internal resistance and the meters to be ideal.

By Kirchhoff's second law:
$$12.0 = V_{\text{LDR}} + V_{50\,\Omega}\;\Rightarrow\; V_{50\,\Omega} = 12.0 - 4 = 8.0\ \mathrm{V}.$$
The current in the series circuit (the ammeter reading) is the current in the $50\ \Omega$ resistor:
$$I = \frac{V_{50\,\Omega}}{R} = \frac{8.0\ \mathrm{V}}{50\ \Omega} = 0.16\ \mathrm{A}.$$

**The ammeter reads $0.16\ \mathrm{A}$.** (At this light intensity the LDR has resistance $4/0.16 = 25\ \Omega$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(f) (i) Calculate the quantity of solar energy which can be captured per unit time by a photovoltaic plate measuring $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ by $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ if the solar constant is $1.4\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Why can all this energy not be converted to electrical energy? *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Solar power captured.** Area of the plate: $A = 6.0\times2.0 = 12\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The solar constant is the power received per unit area, so (assuming the plate faces the sun squarely):
$$P = (\text{solar constant})\times A = 1.4\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\times12\ \mathrm{m^2} = 1.68\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{W}.$$

**About $1.7\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$ of solar energy per second ($16.8\ \mathrm{kW}$).**

**(ii) Why not all converted.** The efficiency of a photovoltaic cell is **well below $100\%$**. Photons with energy smaller than the band gap of the semiconductor (much of the infrared) produce no electron-hole pairs; for photons with energy larger than the band gap, the excess energy is lost as **heat**; part of the light is **reflected** from the surface of the plate; and some energy is lost as heat by the internal resistance of the cell and by electron-hole recombination.
